question: Can a low-dimensional permutation-invariant Gaussian matrix model describe ensembles of neural-network weight matrices throughout training, quantify their departure from initialization, and expose where non-Gaussian corrections become necessary?

key_findings.claim: A 13-parameter permutation-invariant Gaussian matrix model compresses the first- and second-order statistics of square dense-layer weights while preserving correlations forbidden by an i.i.d. Gaussian.
key_findings.evidence: The diagonal action of the neuron-permutation group decomposes the matrix representation into irreducible sectors. Thirteen linear/quadratic graph invariants determine means and covariance blocks, replacing the generic multivariate Gaussian's order-N^4 covariance parameters with a fixed interpretable set.

anchors.section: 2.3 Symmetry in Neural Networks and PIGMMs

key_findings.claim: On the 10-by-10 MNIST network, training moves weights far from the simple i.i.d. initialization law while a correlated Gaussian fit remains accurate late in training.
key_findings.evidence: Across 1,000 independently initialized runs, linear/quadratic invariant deviations from the simple Gaussian increase substantially. Yet 39 held-out cubic/quartic invariant deviations predicted from the fitted PIGMM fall below one standard deviation by the end of training for both Gaussian and uniform initialization, which is the paper's main goodness-of-fit check.

key_findings.claim: The derived Wasserstein metric tracks smooth movement in fitted distribution space but measures distance between Gaussian surrogates rather than between the empirical weight ensembles themselves.
key_findings.evidence: The paper specializes the closed-form 2-Wasserstein distance between Gaussians to the representation blocks of PIGMMs. It reports monotonic distance from initialization in the unregularized runs and altered, sometimes non-monotone trajectories under L2 regularization. Because the inputs are fitted means/covariances, higher-order misspecification is invisible to this distance.

key_findings.claim: Increasing width is a falsification case for a fixed 13-parameter Gaussian: specific cubic and quartic observables diverge more strongly as width grows.
key_findings.evidence: For central widths 10, 40, 160, and 640, the fitted model becomes progressively less representative. In particular, the entrywise-cubic I9 and entrywise-quartic I32 deviations grow markedly; Wasserstein distance from the simple Gaussian also grows and does not settle within 50 epochs. The authors propose adding exactly these invariant terms as non-Gaussian perturbations.

key_findings.claim: The empirical scope is deliberately narrow and cannot yet support claims about modern architectures or learned weight laws generally.
key_findings.evidence: All principal experiments use MNIST, square fully connected matrices, 50 training epochs, and ensemble averages over repeated training. The conclusion states that the roughly one-terabyte raw ensemble is not published, and defers non-square matrices, convolutional networks, Transformers, CIFAR, multi-matrix coupling, and broader tasks.

method.core_idea: Fit a symmetry-reduced correlated Gaussian to ensembles of trained weight matrices using graph-indexed invariant moments, then use unfitted higher-order moments and a Gaussian Wasserstein metric as independent diagnostics.
method.mechanism: One thousand replicas of a small dense MNIST classifier produce an ensemble at every layer and epoch. Thirteen permutation-invariant linear/quadratic averages are analytically inverted into PIGMM parameters. Wick's theorem predicts 39 cubic/quartic observables; standardized prediction residuals measure non-Gaussianity. A representation-block formula computes 2-Wasserstein distance between fitted PIGMMs across epochs, initialization schemes, regularization, and widths.
assumptions: Simultaneously relabeling input and output neurons is the relevant diagonal permutation symmetry for the analyzed square layers.
An ensemble across independently initialized training runs is the appropriate object, rather than one trained model's within-matrix empirical distribution.
First- and second-order invariant means can be estimated accurately from 1,000 replicas.
Selected cubic/quartic invariants are sensitive enough to diagnose practically relevant departures from Gaussianity.

techniques.role: Compresses correlated matrix means and covariances into 13 symmetry-organized parameters.
Gives each moment observable an interpretable directed-graph pattern.
Tests Gaussianity by predicting cubic and quartic invariants that were not used for fitting.
Tracks distributional movement between fitted Gaussian ensembles over training.

evaluations.setting: Three 10-by-10 dense layers trained on MNIST for 50 epochs across 1,000 random initializations
evaluations.metric: Standardized deviations of 13 fit moments and 39 held-out cubic/quartic invariants
evaluations.result: Simple-i.i.d. Gaussian fit degrades after training, while the correlated PIGMM's higher-order residuals return below one standard deviation late in training.
evaluations.baseline: The Gaussian or moment-matched uniform initialization law

evaluations.metric: Invariant deviations, Wasserstein trajectory, and final accuracy
evaluations.result: PIGMM remains broadly adequate, but some cubic/quartic terms exceed one deviation and trajectories become non-monotone; mean final accuracy is reported as 0.9068 plus or minus 0.0011.

evaluations.setting: Width sweep of square hidden layers 10, 40, 160, and 640
evaluations.metric: Higher-order standardized deviations and distance from initialization
evaluations.result: Fixed-parameter Gaussian adequacy worsens with width; a small number of specific cubic/quartic invariants dominate the failure.

limitations: The study uses only MNIST and small fully connected networks; no convolutional, attention, language, or challenging dataset validation is supplied.
The diagonal permutation model directly fits square matrices and does not yet handle the common rectangular-layer case.
Ensemble averages across 1,000 complete training runs are expensive and unavailable for a single deployed model.
The raw one-terabyte weight ensemble is available only by request, limiting independent reproduction.
A finite chosen set of higher moments cannot prove that the empirical law is Gaussian.
failure_modes: A model can match all tested invariants while differing on untested high-order or non-polynomial statistics.
Neuron alignment or symmetry breaking across runs can invalidate the diagonal-permutation ensemble assumption.
Averaging across independently trained networks can Gaussianize statistics that are non-Gaussian within individual solutions.
At large width or under different optimizers, the fixed 13 parameters can miss growing higher-order correlations.
Gaussian Wasserstein distance can look smooth even while higher-order empirical structure changes abruptly.
reusable_insights: Fit symmetry-allowed low-order statistics and reserve higher-order invariants as genuine out-of-fit diagnostics.
Use the identity of the largest residual invariant to propose the next minimal model extension.
Distinguish a distribution over trained models from the empirical distribution of parameters inside one model.
A useful scaling claim should track how model residuals, not only predictive accuracy, change with width and training time.
open_questions: Do PIGMM parameters estimated from small ensembles predict generalization, optimization phase, or failure in larger tasks?
How should the symmetry and invariant basis be generalized to rectangular matrices and coupled Q/K/V or MLP blocks?
Are the observed Gaussian residual patterns stable across optimizers, datasets, losses, and random-seed distributions?
Can a sparse non-Gaussian exponential-family extension remain normalizable and computationally tractable?

competitive_landscape.title: Traditional and Heavy-Tailed Self Regularization in Neural Network Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Martin and Mahoney characterize trained layers through empirical singular-value spectra and heavy-tailed universality classes across practical networks. PIGMM instead models entry correlations across training replicas under permutation symmetry; its Gaussian conclusion concerns a different ensemble and statistic.

competitive_landscape.title: Random matrix analysis of deep neural network weight matrices
competitive_landscape.difference: Thamm et al. test universal singular-value and eigenvector statistics inside trained networks and isolate informative outlier modes. The reviewed paper uses graph-indexed entry moments across replicas, gaining interpretable correlations but evaluating a much narrower model family.

competitive_landscape.title: On Random Matrices Arising in Deep Neural Networks: General I.I.D. Case
competitive_landscape.difference: Pastur and Slavin prove spectral universality for products involving i.i.d. synaptic matrices near initialization. PIGMM empirically studies trained parameter ensembles and finds width-dependent non-Gaussian corrections rather than assuming independent entries.

competitive_landscape.title: Heavy-Tailed Regularization of Weight Matrices in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Heavy-tailed regularization treats spectral tail diagnostics as a trainable prior linked to generalization. PIGMM offers a Gaussian symmetry-reduced descriptive model and suggests invariant perturbations, but does not yet turn them into a training objective or show predictive utility.

novelty_assessment: The distinctive contribution is applying a 13-parameter permutation-invariant Gaussian matrix model to full training ensembles, deriving its Wasserstein geometry, and using graph-indexed held-out moments to localize failures. Random-matrix analysis of neural weights and Gaussian wide-network theory are well established; this paper changes the ensemble, symmetry, and observable basis rather than replacing that prior literature.
reviewer_notes: Read the 61-page extraction including representation-theoretic construction, MNIST ensemble protocol, invariant tables, regularization and width falsification studies, Wasserstein appendix, and outlook. Primary competing arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23. The word Gaussian is scoped to the across-run symmetry-reduced model and its tested moments, not asserted for every trained model or architecture.
